verdict: Winner: Neighbour AI (each light also hears its neighbours). With it, a car loses 109 seconds on average, 52% less than with today's fixed timers.
Independent AI (each light decides alone): 109 seconds, about the same as the winner, 52% less than today.
Central AI (one brain runs all 12 lights): 146 seconds, 35% more delay than the winner, 36% less than today.
Your two ideas side by side: the independent AI had less delay in 15 of 16 situations (4 seasons × 4 times of day), the central AI in 1.
Independent vs neighbour AI: 6 wins to 10. Letting the lights hear their neighbours barely helps on these 12 lights.
Compared with the simple rule that needs no AI (green to the longest queue): Independent AI and Neighbour AI clearly beat it. Central AI does worse than it (146 s vs 138 s).

Would more practice save the central AI? With 4 times more training it got 163 s instead of 146 s: 11% worse. The problem is the design, not practice: one brain has to pick settings for all 12 lights at once (about 16.8 million combinations) from one shared score, so it cannot tell which light did well.
Safety rules off for the independent AI: delay per car 109 → 112 s, longest wait 209 → 300 s, stuck cars removed 0.4 → 0.9 per hour.
Safety rules off for the central AI: delay per car 146 → 493 s, longest wait 215 → 875 s, stuck cars removed 1.3 → 55.5 per hour.
Safety rules off for the neighbour AI: delay per car 109 → 107 s, longest wait 182 → 253 s, stuck cars removed 0.3 → 0.7 per hour.
Best learning method (delay per car, lower is better): Independent AI: PPO 109 s, A2C 112 s, DQN 123 s; Central AI: PPO 146 s, A2C 182 s; Neighbour AI: PPO 109 s, A2C 118 s, DQN 121 s.
